t: A Fun Way To Get Students Engaged In Great Discussions ussions/
q: One of the challenges of group work is getting students to actively participate in discussions.
Mix your students randomly into groups of three or four and be sure to switch them often.
Have each group select one person to pretend to be an extraterrestrial who has just arrived on Earth, and one person to be a translator who speaks the ET’s language.
A variation of the game is to remove the translator. See if they can communicate using only movements, expressions, and body language .
The ET game is an improvisational exercise that has a unique way of drawing students out of their shell.
After just one session of playing the game, you’ll notice an increase in participation.

t: How To Ask For And Receive Your Students’ Attention Within Two Seconds ttention-within-two-seconds/
q: The ability to ask for and receive your students’ attention is crucial.
This underscores the importance of selling not just your lessons, but anything and everything you want your students to be able to do well.
The biggest mistake teachers make is allowing students more time than they need to respond. This is key.
Your students need to see exactly what giving you their attention looks like.
In the past, I’ve used “hey, hey, whaddya say,” “murmur, murmur,” and “blah, blah, blah,” as well as a few others. The goofier, the better.
It saves loads of time, improves listening , encourages group responsibility, and allows you to have instant and total control of your class anytime you need it.

t: How To Handle Six Disrespectful Students In One Class -one-class/
q: One or two disrespectful students are hard enough. How do you handle a half dozen who are determined to make your life miserable?
You see, one of the most common mistakes teachers make is trying to handle difficult students as distinct entities, separate from the class as a whole.
But these individualized methods only make matters worse—because they encourage misbehavior.
The truth is, when you have several or more students who consistently disrupt learning and behave disrespectfully, it’s a sign you’ve lost control of your class—or never had it to begin with.
It’s a classroom management problem, not an individual student problem.
Your most well-behaved students will respond first. You’ll notice them smiling more and making eye contact with you.
You’ve made the gap between the experience of being part of the class, and the experience of being held accountable, so wide that no student can resist.

t: How To Earn Back The Trust Of A Student You’ve Hurt Or Disappointed uve-hurt-or-disappointed/
q: The problem—besides making several critical accountability errors—was that she got it wrong.
It’s best to pull the student aside, look them in the eye, and apologize.
It’s a mistake to be lighthearted or overly friendly with the student you’ve hurt or disappointed.
An apology is the only honest and reliable way to erase any resentment the student may be feeling toward you. But it must come with no strings attached.
To that end, admit that you messed up, that you handled it poorly or shouldn’t have said what you said. Take no more than 30 seconds, and then say the critical words: “I’m sorry.
Students—and people in general—are more likely to accept an apology, and therefore truly forgive, when there is no pressure for them to do so.
By confessing our mistakes, by apologizing when we’re wrong and taking responsibility when we hurt others, we become better people and better teachers.
